content_metadata.description: A video tutorial on how to test for the presence of specific negative ions: carbonate, sulfate, and nitrate, through various chemical reactions and laboratory techniques.

qAndA.question: What color does limewater turn in the presence of carbon dioxide?
What is the chemical formula of the white precipitate formed when testing for sulfates?
What two chemicals are added to a nitrate solution when testing for nitrates?
What color does damp red litmus paper turn in the presence of ammonia?

qAndA.answer: Reduction. The nitrate ion (NO3-) is reduced to an ammonium ion (NH4+).
qAndA.question: What type of chemical reaction occurs when aluminum powder is added to a nitrate solution?

activities.description: The narrator introduces the topic: Testing for negative ions.
The narrator explains how to test for carbonates.
The narrator mentions that dilute acid is added to a test tube.
The narrator explains that the gas produced is bubbled through limewater.
The narrator explains that the reaction releases carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
The narrator explains that many carbonates are insoluble in water.
The narrator explains how to test for sulfates.
The narrator explains that a few drops of barium chloride solution are added to a test tube.
The narrator explains that the white precipitate formed is barium sulfate.
The narrator asks the viewer to write down the equations for the reactions and balance them.
The narrator explains that carbonate ions react with acid to produce carbon dioxide gas and water.
The narrator explains that barium ions and sulfate ions combine to produce a barium sulfate precipitate.
The narrator explains how to test for nitrates.
The narrator explains that sodium hydroxide and aluminum powder are added to a test tube and heated gently in a warm water bath.
The narrator explains that aluminum powder reduces the nitrate ion to an ammonium ion.
The narrator explains that the ammonium ion then reacts with hydroxide to release ammonia.
The narrator explains that ammonia can be tested using a damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.
The narrator explains that you can dip a glass rod in concentrated hydrochloric acid and place it near the mouth of the reaction vessel.
The narrator explains that this should produce ammonium chloride in the form of white smoke if ammonia is present.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In this lesson, you will learn how to test for the presence of carbonate, sulfate,
and nitrate ions.
To test for carbonates, add dilute acid and bubble the gas produced through lime water.
This reaction releases carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky due to the formation
of calcium carbonate.
Since many carbonates are insoluble in water, you will likely be working with solids instead
of solutions.
To test for sulfates, add a few drops of barium chloride solution.
The white precipitate form is barium sulfate, noted for its insoluability in water.
Write down the equations for the above reactions and resume the lesson once you are done.
Remember to balance the equations and use the correct state symbols.
Carbonate ions react with acid to produce carbon dioxide gas and water.
Barium ions and sulfate ions combine to produce a barium sulfate precipitate.
To test for nitrates, add sodium hydroxide and aluminum powder and heat gently in a warm
water bath.
Aluminum powder reduces the nitrate ion to an ammonium ion.
The ammonium ion then reacts with hydroxide to release ammonia.
Ammonia can be tested using a damp red litmus paper, which turns blue.
You can dip a glass rod in concentrated hydrochloric acid and place it near the mouth of the reaction
vessel.
This should produce ammonium chloride in the form of white smoke if ammonia is present.
The production of carbon dioxide from the addition of a dilute acid confirms the presence
of carbonates.
If a white precipitate is formed from the addition of an aqueous barium solution, this means
that sulfates are present.
Nitrates can be reduced to ammonium ions, which can then react with hydroxide ions to produce
ammonia.
Ammonia turns damp red litmus paper blue and forms a white smoke of ammonium chloride
in the presence of concentrated hydrochloric acid.
